questions.prompt: In this zone file, what does the '@' symbol stand for?
choices: The zone origin — example.com. itself (the apex)
A wildcard matching any hostname
The local nameserver
A comment marker
questions.explanation: '@' is shorthand for the current $ORIGIN — here example.com. itself, also called the zone apex. So these lines define the SOA, an NS, and an A record for the bare domain. Wildcards are written as '*', and comments start with ';'.

questions.prompt: How long may resolvers cache the www record defined here, in seconds?
questions.answer_display: 300 seconds (the explicit TTL overrides the $TTL 3600 default)
questions.explanation: A per-record TTL (300) beats the zone default set by $TTL (3600). So www may be cached for 5 minutes, while ftp — which has no explicit TTL — inherits the 3600-second default.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? This zone fails to load.
accept: cname cannot coexist with soa and ns
you can't put a cname at the apex
questions.answer_display: A CNAME at the zone apex — CNAME can't coexist with the SOA/NS records that must live there
questions.explanation: A CNAME makes its name an alias for another and forbids any OTHER record data at that name (RFC 2181 §10.1). The apex must carry SOA and NS records, so an apex CNAME is illegal and loaders reject it. Workarounds: plain A/AAAA records, provider-proprietary ALIAS/ANAME flattening, or an HTTPS record (RFC 9460) for web traffic.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? After loading this zone, blog.example.com resolves to a bizarre name instead of working.
questions.answer_display: Missing trailing dot — the target is treated as relative, becoming myblog.wordpress.com.example.com.
questions.explanation: In a zone file, any name NOT ending in a dot is relative to $ORIGIN. 'myblog.wordpress.com' therefore expands to 'myblog.wordpress.com.example.com.' — the single most classic zone-file bug. Write 'myblog.wordpress.com.' (with the trailing dot) for an absolute name.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? After this edit was deployed to the primary, the secondaries never picked up the change.
accept: the new serial is lower than the old one
questions.answer_display: The SOA serial went BACKWARDS (2026082401 → 2026010100), so secondaries think they're up to date
questions.explanation: Secondaries transfer the zone only when the primary's serial is NEWER (in serial-number arithmetic, RFC 1982). Someone fat-fingered the date-based serial back to January, so every secondary sees 'nothing new' and keeps serving stale data. Fix: bump the serial above the old value on the primary and reload; in stubborn cases, temporarily set it very high or rebuild the secondaries.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? named-checkzone rejects this zone.
accept: cname cannot coexist with other records
cname and mx at the same name
www has both a cname and an mx
questions.answer_display: 'www' has both a CNAME and an MX — a CNAME may not coexist with any other record at the same name
questions.explanation: RFC 2181 §10.1 (following RFC 1034): if a name has a CNAME, that must be its ONLY data. The alias fully redirects the name, so an MX sitting beside it is unreachable/contradictory and loaders refuse it. Either move the MX to the canonical name (webfarm) or replace the CNAME with an A record.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? This is the child zone as published. External resolvers intermittently fail to resolve anything under example.com.
accept: ns2 is missing its a record
questions.answer_display: ns2.example.com is delegated as a nameserver but has no A/AAAA record — an in-bailiwick NS with no address (and no glue)
questions.explanation: ns2 is in-bailiwick (inside the zone it serves), so resolvers can only find its address via glue at the parent or an A/AAAA record in this zone — and there is neither. Whenever a resolver picks ns2, resolution dead-ends; whenever it picks ns1, things work. That coin-flip is your 'intermittent'. Add 'ns2 IN A <ip>' and make sure matching glue exists at the registrar.

questions.prompt: What is the record at this underscore-prefixed name used for?
choices: Email authentication policy — DMARC tells receivers to reject mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment, and where to send reports
Marking the zone as DNSSEC-signed
A service-discovery pointer for mail clients
Verifying domain ownership for a SaaS provider
questions.explanation: _dmarc.<domain> TXT holds the DMARC policy (RFC 7489): p=reject instructs receiving mail servers to refuse messages claiming to be from example.com that fail SPF/DKIM alignment, and rua= collects aggregate reports. The leading underscore follows RFC 8552's convention for protocol-scoped names — it can never collide with a real hostname, since underscores are invalid in those.

questions.prompt: Given this zone, what does a query for www.example.com return?
choices: 203.0.113.10 — an explicit record always beats the wildcard; '*' only synthesizes answers for names that don't exist
Both addresses, in round-robin order
198.51.100.99 — the wildcard matches everything including www
NXDOMAIN — the wildcard and explicit record conflict
questions.explanation: A wildcard is a synthesis rule for NONEXISTENT names only (RFC 4592). www exists, so its own record answers and the wildcard never enters the picture — even for other TYPES at www (querying www MX here yields NODATA, not the wildcard). Also worth knowing: anything.www.example.com isn't covered either once www exists. Wildcards are subtler than they look; treat them with suspicion.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? Mail delivery from some senders fails outright.
accept: the mx points to an ip address
mx must point to a hostname
mx target must be a name not an ip
mx cannot contain an ip literal
questions.answer_display: The MX target is an IP address — it must be a HOSTNAME (that has A/AAAA records), never an IP literal
questions.explanation: MX RDATA is a preference plus a domain name. '192.0.2.25' here isn't parsed as an address — it's read as the HOSTNAME 192.0.2.25 (and being dotless-relative, may even expand to 192.0.2.25.example.com.). Strict MTAs fail to resolve it and bounce or defer mail; lenient ones mask the bug until they don't. Fix: 'MX 10 mail' plus 'mail IN A 192.0.2.25'. (Same rule for NS and CNAME targets: names, never IPs.)

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? SPF checks for this domain return PermError and mail is getting rejected.
questions.answer_display: TWO v=spf1 records — RFC 7208 makes multiple SPF records an automatic PermError; they must be merged into one
questions.explanation: A domain gets exactly one SPF record. When a receiver finds two strings starting 'v=spf1', RFC 7208 §3.2 mandates PermError — it does NOT pick one or merge them, and with DMARC p=reject a PermError can bounce all your mail. This happens constantly when a second provider's 'just add our SPF record' instructions get followed literally. Merge into one: "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.0/24 include:_spf.google.com -all". (The site-verification TXT is fine — only v=spf1 strings count.)

questions.prompt: This SPF record is syntactically valid, yet some receivers return PermError. Why?
choices: It exceeds SPF's limit of 10 DNS lookups — each include/a/mx/ptr costs lookups, and includes pull in their own nested includes
SPF records may list at most 5 include mechanisms
The ptr mechanism is forbidden and voids the record
The record exceeds 255 characters and gets truncated
questions.explanation: RFC 7208 §4.6.4 caps SPF evaluation at 10 DNS-querying mechanisms (include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect) — counted RECURSIVELY, so include:_spf.google.com alone burns several via its nested includes. Eight includes plus a, mx and ptr blows well past 10 → PermError at strict receivers. This is the most common SPF failure in the wild as SaaS senders accumulate. Fixes: prune dead vendors, use ip4:/ip6: literals (they cost zero lookups), or an SPF-flattening service. (ptr is also 'do not use' per the RFC — slow and unreliable — but the lookup limit is what breaks this record.)

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? During a 6-hour primary outage, the secondaries stopped answering for the zone entirely.
accept: the expire timer is too short
expire must be much larger than refresh
questions.answer_display: EXPIRE (3600 = 1 hour) is shorter than REFRESH (24h) — secondaries discard the zone after one hour without primary contact
questions.explanation: EXPIRE is the dead-man's switch: how long a secondary keeps serving the zone after its last successful SOA check against the primary. At 3600s, one hour into the outage every secondary declared its copy too stale and started answering SERVFAIL — turning a primary outage into a total DNS outage, the exact thing secondaries exist to prevent. Sanity order: retry < refresh << expire; RFC 1912 suggests expire of 2-4 weeks (1209600-2419200).

questions.prompt: How does this DNAME behave differently from a CNAME — what exactly gets redirected?
choices: DNAME rewrites every name BELOW legacy (www.legacy → www.newsite.example.net.) but not legacy itself — which is why the A record beside it is legal
DNAME is just a CNAME that's allowed to coexist with other records
DNAME redirects legacy and everything below it, making the A record an error
DNAME copies all records from newsite.example.net into this zone
questions.explanation: DNAME (RFC 6672) substitutes the SUBTREE: anything.legacy.example.com is rewritten to anything.newsite.example.net, with the server synthesizing CNAMEs for old clients. The owner name itself is NOT redirected — legacy.example.com still answers from its own records, hence the perfectly legal A record beside it (illegal next to a CNAME). Classic uses: renamed domains, and ip6.arpa reverse-tree grafting. One footgun: you can't DNAME the zone apex to delegate 'the whole domain'.

questions.prompt: This is a Response Policy Zone loaded by a resolver. What does the 'CNAME .' on the second entry make the resolver do?
choices: Return NXDOMAIN for evil-tracker.io — 'CNAME .' is RPZ's encoding for 'pretend this name doesn't exist'
Redirect the query to the DNS root servers
Strip the CNAME and return an empty answer (NODATA)
Forward the query to localhost for logging
questions.explanation: In RPZ, policy actions are encoded as special CNAME targets: 'CNAME .' → answer NXDOMAIN, 'CNAME *.' → NODATA, 'CNAME rpz-passthru.' → let it through untouched (the allowlist entry here), 'CNAME rpz-drop.' → drop silently, and a real A/CNAME target → walled-garden redirect. So this resolver makes evil-tracker.io and everything under malware-cdn.net vanish for its clients. RPZ is 'DNS firewall as a zone file' — distributed to resolvers by ordinary zone transfer, which is how threat-intel feeds ship blocklists.
